title: Baseline retest for cores/bench
Iterative radix-2 divider off the EX critical path + single shared 33x33 signed multiplier
motivation:
Fmax is 5.442 MHz. The Gowin worst path (199.8 ns, 156 cells) is
clock -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu -> u_ex: the forwarding mux feeding the
fully combinational 32-bit `/` and `%` operators in alu.sv (DIV, DIVU, REM,
REMU, each with its own signed/unsigned array divider). A 32-stage ripple
subtract/restore array is ~32 carry chains in series, which alone is two
orders of magnitude slower than every other path in this 5-stage pipeline.
Disassembling bench/programs/coremark.elf shows exactly 5 div/divu/rem/remu
instructions, all inside main() (setup sizing and post-stop reporting);
none are in iterate()/core_bench_list/matrix/state/crc, i.e. the timed
region between the 0x10000100/0x10000104 markers executes ~zero divides.
Paying a ~34-cycle latency per divide therefore costs ~0 IPC,
while removing the array divider should raise Fmax by an integer factor.
The same ALU also instantiates three separate 64-bit products
(mul_ss, mul_uu, mul_su), tripling DSP usage and adding a wide result mux
on the path the divider currently hides; after the divider goes, that is
the next-longest EX path, so it is folded into the same change.
(test_alu.py shows a multi-cycle div FSM existed under hyp-20260427-002
before the v2 reset, so the approach already passed cosim in this repo.)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
1. New module rtl/divider.sv: a sequential radix-2 non-restoring (or
   restoring) unsigned divider with start/busy/done handshake.
     - On start it latches the post-forward operands and op
       (DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU), takes |a|, |b| for the signed ops and records
       the quotient/remainder sign (q_neg = a[31]^b[31] for DIV,
       r_neg = a[31] for REM).
     - Special cases resolve on the start cycle with no iterations:
       b==0 -> quotient 0xFFFFFFFF / remainder a; signed INT_MIN / -1 ->
       quotient 0x80000000 / remainder 0.
     - Otherwise 32 iterations of one shift-subtract step per cycle
       (33-bit subtractor, 1 carry chain), then a fix-up cycle that
       conditionally negates the result. Result is held in a register;
       `done` stays high until the pipeline consumes it.
     - Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the unit keeps the same
       start/busy/done FSM but completes after ONE busy cycle and returns
       the ALTOPS stand-ins ((a-b)^32'h7f8529ec for DIV, ^32'h10e8fd70
       DIVU, ^32'h8da68fa5 REM, ^32'h3138d0e1 REMU), computed from the
       latched operands. This keeps the liveness/insn/reg checks inside
       the depth-20 BMC budget while still exercising the EX-stall path
       formally.
2. alu.sv: delete the combinational `/` and `%` arms (DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU
   return 32'b0 from the ALU; the EX stage selects the divider result for
   those ops). Replace mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su with ONE signed 33x33 product:
     a_ext = {a[31] & (op==MULH || op==MULHSU), a}
     b_ext = {b[31] & (op==MULH), b}
     prod  = $signed(a_ext) * $signed(b_ext)   // 66-bit, low 64 used
     MUL -> prod[31:0], MULH/MULHSU/MULHU -> prod[63:32]
   Gowin maps this onto one MULT36X36-class DSP instead of three, and
   the output mux collapses to a 2:1 lo/hi select. Keep the ALTOPS arms
   for MUL/MULH/MULHU/MULHSU exactly as they are today.
3. ex_stage.sv: instantiate the divider. is_div = in.valid &&
   alu_op in {DIV,DIVU,REM,REMU}. Start the divider when is_div and the
   unit is idle (not already started for this instruction). Export
   ex_busy = is_div && !div_done. When ex_busy and no dmem stall, the
   EX/MEM register captures a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0,
   mem_read=0, mem_write=0, is_branch/is_jump=0) instead of the
   instruction; when div_done and the EX/MEM register advances, it
   captures the divider result as alu_result and the divider returns to
   idle (so the same instruction is never restarted). dmem stall keeps
   its existing precedence (EX/MEM hold) — the divider just keeps its
   done result until the stall clears.
4. hazard_unit.sv: add input ex_busy. stall_if |= ex_busy,
   stall_id |= ex_busy; flush_id must NOT fire because of ex_busy
   (redirect cannot be asserted while a divide sits in EX; load-use
   against a younger instruction in IF must not bubble ID/EX while EX is
   held — gate load_use's flush with !ex_busy as is done for
   dmem_stall).
5. id_stage.sv (operand refresh): while EX is held (ex_busy or
   dmem_stall) the producers ahead of the divide drain out of EX/MEM and
   MEM/WB, so the forwarding sources disappear and ID/EX.rs?_val is
   stale. Add an `ex_hold` input plus the EX stage's post-forward rs1/rs2
   values; when ex_hold, write reg_q.rs1_val/rs2_val <= forwarded rs1/rs2
   (all other ID/EX fields hold). This keeps RVFI rs1_rdata/rs2_rdata and
   the divider's latched operands architecturally correct regardless of
   how long the stall lasts, and it's a 2:1 mux on the ID/EX D-input, not
   on any long path.
6. core.sv: wire ex_busy from u_ex into u_hazard, the refresh path into
   u_id, and list divider.sv in the rtl glob (no port changes on `core`).
Expected result: the 200 ns divider path disappears. The new critical
path should be one of forward-mux -> 33x33 DSP multiply -> EX/MEM,
forward-mux -> 32-bit branch compare -> redirect -> PC / ID/EX flush, or
imem_data -> decoder/regfile LUT-RAM -> ID/EX, each in the ~15-30 ns
range on GW2AR-18 — i.e. Fmax in the ~35-60 MHz region versus 5.4 MHz.
IPC loss is bounded by (#divides in timed region x ~34 cycles), which is
well under 1% of CoreMark cycles. Net fitness gain is far above the
schema cap of +50%.

The baseline runs at 5.442 MHz. Gowin's worst path is 199.8 ns (156 cells):
clock -> u_fwd -> u_ex -> u_ex/u_alu -> u_ex, which is the fully combinational

EX/MEM register. Every other EX path (adder, shifter, compare, forwarding
mux) is roughly one order of magnitude shorter. CoreMark at -O3 executes
very few DIV/REM instructions in the timed region, so the divider sets Fmax
for the whole core while contributing almost nothing to IPC. The multiplier
is next: alu.sv instantiates three separate 64-bit products (ss, uu, su),
which becomes three DSP cascades plus fabric adders and a 3-way select.
Fitness = iter/cycle x Fmax, so removing the divider from the single-cycle
path is worth far more than any IPC tweak right now.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure the M-extension datapath:

1. New module rtl/div_unit.sv: a sequential radix-2 restoring (or non-restoring)
   divider, 1 quotient bit per cycle (~33 cycles), working on absolute values
   with a final sign fixup. Handshake: `start` (valid DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU in
   ID/EX and unit idle, not already done), `busy`, `done`, `result`. On `start` it
   LATCHES the post-forward rs1/rs2 values (forward sources drain out of
   EX/MEM and MEM/WB while EX is stalled, so the operands must be captured at
   start; the latched values also feed EX/MEM rs1_val/rs2_val/write_data for
   RVFI). `done` stays asserted and the result is held until the pipeline
   actually advances out of EX (i.e. done && !stall_ex_mem), so a dmem stall
   that happens on the completion cycle cannot lose the result.
   Corner cases (RV32M): b==0 -> quotient 0xFFFFFFFF with NO sign fixup of
   the quotient, remainder = a; INT_MIN / -1 falls out of the abs algorithm
   (|INT_MIN| = 0x80000000, /1, negate -> 0x80000000, rem 0) but test it
   explicitly. Optional early-out for b==0 (finish in 1 cycle).
   Under `ifdef RISCV_FORMAL_ALTOPS` the unit keeps the same start/done
   handshake but completes after 1 cycle with the ALTOPS formulas
   ((a-b) ^ const, same constants as today) so formal still exercises the
   stall/hold/forwarding path while fitting liveness depth 20 in checks_si.cfg.

2. rtl/alu.sv: delete the combinational `/` and `%` arms (DIV/DIVU/REM/REMU
   return don't-care/0 from the ALU; the ALTOPS arms for DIV* also move to
   div_unit). Replace mul_ss/mul_uu/mul_su with ONE signed 33x33 multiply:
     a_ext = {a[31] & (op==MULH || op==MULHSU), a}
     b_ext = {b[31] & (op==MULH), b}
     prod  = $signed(a_ext) * $signed(b_ext)   // 66-bit
     MUL -> prod[31:0]; MULH/MULHU/MULHSU -> prod[63:32]
   This maps to a single Gowin MULT36X36 and removes the 3-way product mux.
   Keep the ALTOPS MUL* arms unchanged.

3. rtl/ex_stage.sv: instantiate div_unit; select EX/MEM.alu_result =
   is_div ? div_result : (is_jump ? pc+4 : alu_result). While a divide is
   in EX and not done, EX/MEM captures a bubble (valid=0, reg_write=0,
   mem_read=0, mem_write=0) instead of the instruction. When done, capture the
   real divide with the latched operands.

4. rtl/hazard_unit.sv: new input div_stall = (ID/EX holds a valid DIV-class
   op) && !div_done. div_stall -> stall_if=1 (hold PC), stall_id=1 (HOLD
   ID/EX, not flush), and must not assert flush_id. Redirect cannot
   coincide (branches/jumps are younger and still in IF/ID). dmem_stall
   keeps priority over everything as today.

5. rtl/decoder.sv / core_pkg.sv: add ctrl bit `is_div` (set for funct7=0x01,
   funct3[2]=1) so EX does not have to decode alu_op ranges on the critical
   path. is_illegal default stays 1; nothing about trap discipline changes.

Expected effect: the 200 ns path disappears. The new worst path should be
forward-mux -> 33x33 DSP multiply (or the adder/branch-compare -> redirect ->
PC path) at roughly 25-40 ns, i.e. Fmax ~25-40 MHz vs 5.4 MHz. The IPC cost
is ~33 cycles per executed divide; objdump of bench/programs/coremark.elf
shows only 5 static divides (all DIVU, all inside main(): iteration/size
setup and result reporting, not in the list/matrix/state/crc kernels) vs
16 MUL + 12 MULHU. So divides in the timed region are ~0 and iter/cycle
should be essentially unchanged; the multiplier stays single-cycle because
MUL/MULHU do appear in the kernels. Area also drops a lot (four
32-level divider arrays are most of the 12.3k LUTs). Even a pessimistic
20 MHz is a >3x fitness gain; the schema caps the estimate at +50%.

title: IF-stage predecode + 64-entry bimodal BHT: zero-bubble taken branches and JAL
motivation:
Every taken control transfer is resolved in EX and costs exactly 2 bubble
cycles (the IF and ID slots are squashed; target fetched at t+3 instead of
t+1). Measured with test/cosim/reference.py on bench/programs/coremark.elf
over the timed (start/stop marker) region: 2,922,015 retired instrs,
~4.49M cycles (CPI ~1.54 at the current 12.12 iter/s, 5.442 MHz).
  - conditional branches 529,588 (18.1%), taken 294,425 (10.1%)
    (backward 287,132 of which 235,191 taken; forward taken 59,234)
  - JAL 49,367 (1.7%), JALR 13,735 (0.47%, all returns)
=> (294,425 + 49,367 + 13,735) x 2 = ~715K cycles = ~16% of all cycles are
redirect bubbles. Fmax is pinned at ~5.4 MHz by the combinational divider
(fwd -> ALU div -> EX/MEM, 199.8 ns), so front-end prediction logic is far
off the critical path; in the timed netlist io_imemData is an LFSR register
and io_imemAddr is the PC register, so an IF predecode is a short reg->reg
path. Iterations/cycle is the lever.
Offline trace simulation of direction predictors on the same trace:
  - static BTFN:                111,175 mispredicts (21.0%)
  - bimodal 2-bit, 32 entries:   55,556
  - bimodal 2-bit, 64 entries:   51,419 (9.7%)
  - bimodal 2-bit, 256 entries:  44,266
64 entries is the knee (128 flops); RAS would only recover ~27K cycles
(0.6%) and is left out to keep risk low.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Predict next-PC in IF using the combinationally-returned instruction
(io_imemData belongs to the same cycle as io_imemAddr=pc):
  - Predecode opcode: JAL (1101111) -> always predict taken;
    BRANCH (1100011) -> predict taken iff BHT[pc[7:2]][1] == 1.
  - pred_target = pc + (is_jal ? J-imm : B-imm) (one 32-bit adder with an
    imm mux built straight from instr bits).
  - Never predict when the target is misaligned (imm[1] != 0), so the
    existing EX misalign-trap path (no redirect, pc_next = pc+4) is
    untouched. JALR and everything else predict pc+4 as today.
  - PC update priority: redirect (EX mispredict) > stall hold >
    (pred_taken ? pred_target : pc+4). pred_taken is forced 0 in the
    IF/ID bundle whenever the slot is flushed (redirect / imem stall), so
    the bit captured into ID/EX always matches the PC choice made in the
    same cycle (PC advances iff ID/EX captures the IF instruction).
BHT: 64 x 2-bit saturating counters in flops, reset to 2'b01 (weakly
not-taken), read asynchronously by IF at pc[7:2], updated from EX with
in.pc[7:2] and the actual outcome when in.valid && is_branch && the
EX/MEM register is advancing (not during dmem stall, so held branches do
not double-count).
EX resolves mispredicts generically (covers illegal-funct3 "branches"
that predecode may have predicted):
  actual_taken = (branch_taken || is_jump) && !misalign_fault
  redirect     = is_jalr ? !misalign_fault
                         : (actual_taken != pred_taken)
  redirect_target = actual_taken ? (is_jump ? jump_target : branch_target)
                                 : pc + 4
pc_next / all RVFI fields stay computed from the architectural outcome, so
retirement order, pc_rdata/pc_wdata chaining and trap behaviour are
unchanged; only which wrong-path slots get squashed changes.
Estimated savings: branches (294,425 - 51,419) x 2 = 486K + JAL 49,367 x 2
= 99K => ~585K of 4.49M cycles (13%) => ~+15% iter/cycle with Fmax
unchanged (divider stays critical). Expect ~+12..15% fitness after P&R
noise.

title: Decouple EX redirect from IF-NOP mux, load-use detect and wide ID/EX flush (narrow valid-only kill)
motivation:
The champion (44.655 MHz, 99.41 iter/s) has its Gowin worst path from
cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s to cpu/u_id/id_ex_w.rs2_val_21_s1 (27.6 ns,
44 cells, 21 logic levels), running through u_id -> u_ex -> u_if ->
u_hazard -> u_id. That is the EX branch/jump resolve (forward mux ->
32-bit compare -> `redirect`), and it does not stop at the PC. Three
more things hang off `redirect`:
  1. if_stage forces `out.instr = redirect ? NOP : imem_data` (a 32-bit

  2. hazard_unit compares ID/EX.rd against that *muxed* instr[19:15] /
     instr[24:20] to get load_use, which feeds stall_id, and
  3. stall_id / flush_id (reset||flush) drive the CE and SR pins of

EX (the only thing that can cause load_use) can never redirect in the
same cycle, so load_use and redirect are mutually exclusive. Killing a
wrong-path instruction also only needs its valid bit and a few
side-effect ctrl bits cleared, not the whole payload.

motivation:

front end combinationally in the same cycle.

44.8 MHz; clock insertion 5.3 ns on both ends) breaks down as:
regfile BSRAM DO (Gowin retimed ID/EX.rs1_val into it) 7.6 ns -> fwd /
alu_a mux 11.9 -> 32-bit comparator carry chain done 14.9 -> branch_cond /
redirect 18.4 -> u_if flush/NOP mux (fanout 102) 19.2 -> NOP-muxed
rs2_addr 20.5 -> hazard load-use compare 22.0 -> u_id flush/stall logic
26.4 (fanout 33) -> ID/EX rs2_val RESET 27.6. i.e. ~9 ns of the path is
redirect -> IF instr NOP mux -> regfile/hazard addresses -> ID/EX reset.

title: Take the 33x33 DSP multiplier off the single-cycle EX path: registered multi-cycle MUL in the divider's start/done handshake
motivation:
The champion (50.73 MHz, 26.61 ns arrival, 16 logic cells) is limited by
cpu/u_rf (regfile BSRAM) -> u_id -> u_ex fwd/operand muxes -> u_ex/u_alu
-> u_ex -> dmem BSRAM address, i.e. the whole EX result path. u_alu
contains a fully combinational signed 33x33 multiply (2 DSP blocks in
MULT36X36 mode) whose low product bits feed the same 13-way result mux
as the adder, then the is_jump/pc+4 mux and the div_out OR, then
EX/MEM.alu_result (which Gowin retimes into the dmem BSRAM address
register). MEASURED with `make timing TARGET=bench` on the champion:
ALL 25 failing setup paths (25.78-26.61 ns) run through
cpu/u_ex/u_alu/prod_65_s1 (the DSP). Worst path: regfile BSRAM DO 7.59
-> rs1 bypass LUT 8.73 -> fwd mux 3 LUTs 10.77 -> alu_a 11.33 ->
u_alu/mul_a_32 (sign-extension bit) 12.40 -> DSP in 14.58 / out 18.34
(3.76 ns cell) -> 6-LUT result/pc+4/div_out mux chain (n767_*) 23.39
-> dmem addr LUT 24.42 -> dmem BSRAM 26.61. The next paths (no DSP)
are nowhere in the top 25; the 32-bit ALU carry chain is ~0.035
ns/bit, so the adder reaches the result mux ~4-5 ns earlier than the
DSP output does.
The multiply is rare in the timed region: CoreMark -O3 has 16 static
MUL + 12 MULHU (+5 DIVU) and the dynamic count is dominated by the
small-N matrix kernels, roughly 15-25K multiplies out of 2.92M
retired instructions (<1%). This is exactly the pattern of the
+720% divider lesson: a rare op held single-cycle on the critical path.

existing sequential M-unit handshake (rtl/divider.sv, renamed in spirit
to a mul/div unit; the file/module name may stay) so the DSP runs

    post-forward operands and the two sign-extension bits into
    mul_a_q/mul_b_q (33-bit, packable into the DSP input registers;
    a_q/b_q already exist for RVFI rs1/rs2_rdata and can be reused
    with 1 extra sign bit each) plus a hi/lo select bit.
  - next cycle: prod_q <= mul_a_q * mul_b_q (DSP output register).
  - then S_DONE: result = hi_q ? prod_q[63:32] : prod_q[31:0] (a

title: Split EX: dedicated AGU for the dmem address + multiplier moved to the MEM stage (mul-use interlock)
motivation:
Gowin timing of the champion (make timing, place_option 0, 26.61 ns
path, 16 cells) shows exactly what limits Fmax:
  regfile BSRAM CLKB->DO[31] (tC2Q 2.26 ns)
  -> u_id rs1_val bypass LUT (write-first mux, retimed behind the BSRAM)
  -> u_ex rs1 forward mux (3 LUT levels) -> alu_a mux
  -> u_alu mul_a sign-extend LUT -> DSP prod_65_s1 A[35]->DOUT (3.76 ns)
  -> 7 LUT levels of ALU result mux / jump pc+4 mux / div OR (n767_*)
  -> dmem_addr LUT -> dmem BSRAM ADB[3] setup.
The bench's dmem is an async-read array, so Gowin absorbs the core's
EX/MEM alu_result flops into the dmem BSRAM address register: the whole
EX datapath including the 33x33 DSP multiply and the 19-way result mux
sits in front of the BSRAM address. Only LOAD/STORE need that address,
and it is always rs1+imm; and only MUL* need the DSP. Roughly 6 ns of
the path is the multiplier (mul_a LUT + route + DSP) and ~6 ns is the
result-mux tail, neither of which a load/store address needs.

  - control mispredicts: ~51K bimodal-BHT branch mispredicts plus ~13.7K
    JALRs (all returns, which always redirect today) at 2-3 cycles each,
    ~0.13-0.2M cycles.
A better direction predictor alone caps out low: even a perfect branch
predictor saves ~51K x 2-3 cycles (~3%), below the 4.6% acceptance bar,
and trace simulation (r1s2) showed a 4x larger bimodal table only removes
~7K mispredicts. The bigger predictor lever is to USE the already-accurate
prediction (JAL always, BHT for branches, now RAS for returns) to let
fetch run ahead of decode. Today the IF-stage prediction only chooses the
next PC in lock-step with ID; every backend stall wastes a delivered
fetch, and every later imem stall is fully exposed. Because the imem and
dmem ready draws are independent, the cycles in which the backend is
stalled but imem is ready (~0.78 x ~0.28M ~= 0.2M) can be banked into a
small queue and later spent to cover imem-stall cycles. With ~90% of
control transfers predicted in IF, the run-ahead stream is almost always
on the correct path (a flush happens only every ~45 instructions, while
an imem stall happens every ~4.5 cycles, so banked entries are nearly
always consumed before a flush).
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the lock-step IF into a small decoupled, prediction-directed fetch
unit, and add a return-address stack so returns stop breaking the run-ahead
stream and stop paying the redirect penalty.

1) Fetch queue (FQ), 2 entries in flops, each {pc[31:0], instr[31:0],
   pred_taken, pred_tgt[31:0]} (pred_tgt only needed for RAS-predicted
   JALR; may be narrowed to [31:2]). Logic lives in if_stage.sv.
   - Fetch fires when  fetch_fire = imem_ready && !fq_full && !redirect_q.
     The fetch PC register advances to the predicted next PC exactly when
     fetch_fire (redirect_q still has top priority and loads
     redirect_target). NOTE: the PC enable no longer depends on load-use,
     dmem_stall or ex_busy at all (those only gate the FQ pop), which also
     removes the hazard_unit -> PC-CE path from the front end.
   - ID source select: if FQ non-empty, ID sees the FQ head
     {pc, instr, valid=1, pred_taken, pred_tgt}; else ID sees the fetched
     word directly (bypass, valid = imem_ready && !redirect_q), exactly as
     today. The regfile read addresses and the hazard_unit load-use compare
     take rs1/rs2 from this selected raw word (fq_nonempty is a flop, so
     this adds a single 2:1 mux level ahead of the regfile/hazard).
   - id_accept = the ID/EX register captures the selected instruction as a
     real (valid) instruction this cycle = src_valid && !stall_id &&
     !load_use && !redirect_q.
     pop  = fq_nonempty && id_accept
     push = fetch_fire && !(fq_empty && id_accept)   (not bypassed)
     count/head/tail update from push/pop (simultaneous push+pop allowed).
   - redirect_q flushes the FQ (count <= 0) and, as today, bubbles ID/EX
     and kills the wrong-path instruction in EX.
   - An instruction whose ID/EX capture is blocked (load-use bubble,
     dmem_stall/ex_busy hold) stays at the FQ head (or, on the bypass
     path, is pushed into the FQ instead of being discarded), so no
     refetch is needed and the fetch PC keeps advancing.
   - The predecode (JAL / BRANCH / RAS return), BHT read and pc+imm adder
     stay on imem_data + fetch PC exactly as today; pred_taken/pred_tgt
     travel with the instruction through the FQ into ID/EX.
   Invariants to keep: in-order delivery; pred_taken of every ID/EX
   instruction equals the next-PC choice made when it was fetched (so the
   EX mispredict check stays exact); ID/EX never captures an FQ entry
   during a redirect_q cycle.

2) Return address stack, 4 entries x 30 bits (pc[31:2]) in flops, with a
   2-bit TOS pointer (circular, overflow overwrites oldest), updated
   speculatively at fetch_fire only (no repair; corruption only costs
   accuracy, correctness comes from EX verification):
   - push pc+4 when the fetched word is JAL or JALR with rd in {x1,x5}
     (the pc+4 adder already exists in IF).
   - predict a return when the fetched word is JALR with rd == x0,
     rs1 in {x1,x5}, imm == 0 (the `ret` idiom GCC -O3 emits): pred_taken=1,
     next PC = pred_tgt = {RAS[top], 2'b00}; pop.
   - EX (ex_stage.sv): for JALR, mispredict =
       (actual_taken != pred_taken) ||
       (actual_taken && pred_taken && jump_target[31:2] != pred_tgt[31:2]).
     Because only imm==0 returns are predicted, the target compare can use
     the forwarded rs1[31:2] directly (in parallel with the JALR adder, same
     depth as the BEQ comparator) and it only feeds the redirect_q D input.
     Misaligned JALR targets: actual_taken=0 via misalign_fault ->
     mispredict when predicted -> redirect to pc_next = pc+4, as today.
     Non-return JALRs keep pred_taken=0 and always redirect as today.

Expected effect on cycles: ~0.2M backend-stall cycles become banked
fetches, most of which later hide an imem stall (-4..5% cycles); RAS
removes most of the ~13.7K return redirects (-0.6..1%). Fmax should be
neutral to slightly positive: the new logic is a flop-selected mux ahead
of decode/regfile addressing and FQ enables, and the PC enable loses its
dependency on the load-use compare and dmem_ready; the EX critical path
(ID/EX operand -> fwd mux -> ALU -> dmem address) is untouched apart from
the RAS compare feeding redirect_q. Net ~+5..7% fitness.

title: Flatten the EX datapath: pre-registered forward hits merged with the regfile bypass into one AND-OR operand mux, plus a flat one-hot ALU result mux
motivation:
The champion (hyp-20260928-002-r3s1, 64.29 MHz, 149.48) has one critical
path in every placement: cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s -> u_id -> u_ex ->
u_ex/u_alu -> u_ex/reg_q.alu_result (20.985 ns arrival, 14 logic cells,
about 15.5 ns of data path). Gowin maps the regfile onto a BSRAM whose read
address register is the raw imem_data[19:15], so ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val are
BSRAM DO pins (tC2Q ~2.26 ns). The EX cycle then chains:
  BSRAM DO -> write-first bypass LUT (the reg_file.sv bypass, retimed
  behind the BSRAM) -> 3-level forward mux, whose select comes from 5-bit
  rd==rs comparators and a priority chain evaluated in EX -> alu_a
  (is_auipc) / alu_b (alu_src) mux -> ALU arm (adder / 3 shifters /
  comparators) -> 11-way case mux on alu_op -> is_jump ? pc+4 mux ->
  "| div_out" OR -> EX/MEM.alu_result.
At most 2-3 of those ~12 LUT levels do arithmetic. The rest are
select/merge levels. Their select inputs could be known a cycle early,
or at least computed from flops in parallel with the BSRAM clock-to-out.
The same operand prefix also feeds the AGU (-> dmem BSRAM address) and the
branch comparator (-> redirect_q), so shortening it helps the next paths
too. This is a pure micro-optimization. The pipeline, hazards and cycle
count stay exactly as they are (CoreMark cycles should stay 4,300,957),
so the whole gain is Fmax.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild the EX select/merge logic so that every mux select is a flop (or
one LUT of flops) and the BSRAM data passes through one operand-merge
LUT level and two result-merge levels. Function stays cycle-for-cycle
identical to today's forward_unit + write-first regfile.

(1) Forward-hit bits computed in ID and registered in ID/EX. In id_stage,
    from the same raw_instr[19:15]/[24:20] fields that address the
    regfile, compute for each of rs1 and rs2:
      nz   = (rs != 0)
      m1   = nz && (id_ex.rd == rs)   // this producer goes to EX/MEM next cycle
      m2   = nz && (ex_mem.rd == rs)  // this producer goes to MEM/WB next cycle
      byp  = nz && wb_w_en && (wb_w_addr == rs) // regfile write this cycle
    Register nz/m1/m2/byp for each rs, plus one shared 32-bit
    wbd_q <= wb_w_data, in ID/EX with the same enable as the data fields
    (load when !stall, also on flush; hold on stall).
    Why this is exact: whenever ID/EX loads, EX/MEM and MEM/WB load on
    the same edge (stall_id >= dmem_stall), so next cycle EX/MEM.rd and
    MEM/WB.rd equal the rds compared here. Under a dmem_stall hold,
    EX/MEM and MEM/WB data are frozen, so the hits stay valid. Under an
    ex_busy hold, EX/MEM fills with ctrl=0 bubbles, which the reg_write
    gating below turns off, and the divider only reads operands on its
    start cycle, as today.
(2) Regfile raw read. Add a parameter to reg_file.sv (e.g.
    WRITE_FIRST=1 by default, so test_reg_file.py is unchanged) and
    instantiate it from core.sv with 0. Then rs?_data = regs[addr], with
    no write-first mux and no x0 mux. x0 is still never written.
    ID/EX.rs?_val captures that raw value, and Gowin can keep the
    BSRAM with nothing retimed behind its DO.
(3) One-hot AND-OR operand mux in EX (replaces forward_unit's comparators
    and the 3-level mux):
      f1 = m1_q & ex_mem.ctrl.reg_write
      f2 = ~f1 & m2_q & mem_wb.ctrl.reg_write
      f3 = ~f1 & ~f2 & byp_q
      f0 = nz_q & ~f1 & ~f2 & ~byp_q
      rs = ({32{f0}} & rf_q) | ({32{f3}} & wbd_q)
         | ({32{f1}} & ex_mem.alu_result) | ({32{f2}} & wb_w_data)
    The reg_write gating reproduces today's behavior for bubbles, stores,
    branches, and the misalign traps that clear reg_write (JAL/JALR in
    EX/MEM, loads in MEM/WB). The selects are 1-2 LUTs of flops, ready
    before BSRAM DO. Write it so the rf_q term enters at the last LUT
    (rf & f0 | pre-ORed rest), which leaves BSRAM DO -> 1 LUT -> ALU.
    Pure rs1/rs2 feed the AGU, branch comparator, divider, store
    write_data and EX/MEM.rs?_val (multiplier operands + RVFI), as
    today.
(4) Fold alu_src into a separate ALU-b copy of the rs2 mux. Also
    register s_imm = alu_src and gate the rs2 hit selects with ~alu_src
    for this copy:
      alu_b = ({32{g0}} & rf2_q) | ... | ({32{s_imm}} & imm_q)
    This removes the alu_b mux level. Drop the alu_a is_auipc mux:
    alu_a = rs1. AUIPC's result comes from the existing in.pc + in.imm
    adder (branch_target) as a result arm (see 5).
(5) Flat one-hot result merge. Register a one-hot result-select vector
    in ID/EX, decoded in id_stage from the unchanged decoder outputs:
    add, sub, sll, srl, sra, slt, sltu, logic(and/or/xor), lui, link
    (JAL/JALR -> pc+4), auipc (-> pc+imm). ADD/AUIPC/JAL must not
    select the adder arm. EX/MEM.alu_result becomes an AND-OR of the
    arms, plus the div_done & div_result term. Pre-OR the non-critical
    arms (logic, lui, link, auipc, slt/sltu, div) off the critical path,
    so that only the adder and the shifters enter the final 1-2 LUT
    levels. This replaces the 11-way case mux, the is_jump mux and the
    separate div OR. alu.sv can keep its (op, a, b) -> out interface for
    test_alu.py by decoding op one-hot internally. If the hierarchy
    blocks flattening, the implementer may move the merge into ex_stage
    and keep alu.sv as a thin wrapper for the test.
Expected effect: EX path from ~14 to ~8-9 cells (BSRAM -> 1 LUT -> carry
chain / shifter -> 2 LUT -> FF), roughly 15.5 -> 11.5-12.5 ns. The next
limiters (IF predecode -> PC, comparator -> redirect_q) probably cap the
gain near 72-78 MHz. IPC is unchanged, so fitness should rise about
+12-18%.
Correctness guard: selects (3) are exactly today's forward_unit
priority (EX/MEM > MEM/WB > regfile-with-write-first), so formal/cosim
behavior is bit-identical. RVFI keeps reporting the pure post-forward
rs1/rs2.

lesson: - 2026-09-28 hyp-20260928-001-r4s0 (regression, +1.44%): Flattening the EX select logic (forward hits precomputed in ID and registered in ID/EX, raw non-write-first BSRAM regfile read, a one-hot AND-OR operand mux with alu_src folded in, and a flat one-hot result merge with the slow arms pre-ORed) kept cycles the same but only moved Fmax from about 64.3 to about 65.2 MHz, against a 72-78 MHz forecast; the likely reason is that Gowin's LUT4 mapping had already absorbed most of those "mux levels" (a 4-source AND-OR per bit still needs 2 LUT4 levels, and a 5-arm result merge still needs 2-3), so forecasts built by counting RTL mux levels overestimate the gain, and the next Fmax attempt should take the BSRAM DO -> adder/shifter arithmetic itself off the path (move the regfile read or forwarding a stage earlier) instead of reshaping the selects.

title: Decode-stage operand bypass: async-read regfile + forwarding into real ID/EX operand flops
motivation:
The champion's worst path (20.985 ns arrival, 14 cells, ~15.5 ns data
path at 64.3 MHz) starts at cpu/u_rf/regs_regs_0_0_s: Gowin mapped the
32x32 regfile onto a BSRAM whose registered read address is the raw
imem_data[19:15] field, so ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val are not flops at all.
They are the BSRAM DO pins (tC2Q ~2.26 ns), followed in EX by the
write-first bypass LUT, the 3-level EX forward mux (select computed in
EX from ID/EX.rs?_addr vs EX/MEM.rd / MEM/WB.rd), the alu_a/alu_b muxes,
and only then the ALU, the result mux and EX/MEM.alu_result. In the
pre-r3s1 report the part before the ALU took ~6 ns (5.33 -> 11.33).

branch comparator (-> redirect_q) and the AGU (-> dmem BSRAM address).

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Change the pipeline so EX starts from real operand flops, VexRiscv-style.
The regfile read and the whole bypass network move into the decode
cycle and the result is registered into ID/EX. The hazard/stall
structure stays as it is, so the CoreMark cycle count should be
identical (4,300,957).
(1) Regfile read in ID. Keep rtl/reg_file.sv's async-read array off
    BSRAM. Primary choice: (* syn_ramstyle = "registers" *) on regs,
    with the synchronous reset kept. That gives identical semantics, and
    test_reg_file.py's reset_clears_all and the zero-initialised
    reference ISS still hold. Keep the x0 read and the write-first
    bypass. The read address stays the raw imem_data[19:15]/[24:20], so
    the regfile data arrives inside the IF/ID cycle: imem BSRAM DO ->
    32:1 flop mux (LUT4 + MUX2_LUT5..8) -> bypass. Only fall back to
    distributed_ram (which has no reset) if the flop mux's high-fanout
    read-address nets make this ID path critical. That would also mean
    editing the reset test.
(2) ID-stage forwarding. Compute the forward selects in ID from the raw
    imem_data rs fields and the registered ID/EX.rd/ctrl.reg_write
    (distance 1) and EX/MEM.rd/ctrl.reg_write (distance 2). They are
    ready early (imem tC2Q + one 5-bit compare). Then mux, per operand:
      - distance 1: EX's combinational result (the value that goes to
        EX/MEM.alu_result: ALU result, pc+4 for JAL/JALR, OR div_out).
      - distance 2: MEM's combinational result, the same value MEM/WB
        captures (is_mul ? mul_out : mem_to_reg ? load_data : alu_result).
      - otherwise: the regfile read. Distance 3 (WB writing this cycle)
        is covered by the regfile's write-first bypass, and anything
        older is in the array.
    Register the result into ID/EX.rs1_val/rs2_val. Also register
    pre-muxed ALU operands ID/EX.alu_a = is_auipc ? pc : rs1_fwd and
    ID/EX.alu_b = alu_src ? imm : rs2_fwd (about 64 new FFs). EX then
    feeds the ALU straight from alu_a/alu_b. The branch comparator,
    AGU (rs1_val + imm), store data, divider operands, EX/MEM
    rs1_val/rs2_val (MUL operands) and RVFI all use rs1_val/rs2_val
    directly.

    rtl/forward_unit.sv file, because test_pipeline.py lists it by
    name, and repurpose it as the ID-side select generator. The
    load-use / mul-use interlock is unchanged: a LOAD/MUL in ID/EX
    bubbles its dependent in ID for one cycle, then forwards from MEM's
    combinational result. dmem stall and ex_busy still hold ID/EX, and
    the operands it holds are already final. The divider's stale-operand
    RVFI workaround (div_a/div_b) can stay as it is.

    fwd mux (2 LUT levels) -> ID/EX flop. EX -> EX/MEM gets shorter.

    LUT, one or two forward-mux levels (the selects are now early) and
    the alu_a/alu_b mux level. Estimate: ~3.5-5 ns off a 15.5 ns data
    path.
  Branch compare -> redirect_q and AGU -> dmem address shrink the same

title: Prediction-directed decoupled fetch: 2-entry fetch queue + 4-entry return-address stack
motivation:
Champion hyp-20260928-002-r3s1 (149.48) runs the timed CoreMark region in
4,300,957 cycles for ~2.92M retired instructions (CPI ~1.47) at 64.3 MHz.
Its critical path (regfile BSRAM -> u_id write-first bypass -> u_ex
forward mux -> ALU -> EX/MEM.alu_result, 21.0 ns) is entirely in EX.
The front end is far off that path. Estimated split of the ~1.38M
overhead cycles:
  - imem stalls: io_imemReady is low on ~22% of cycles, and each one is
    an exposed front-end bubble whenever the backend could have taken an
    instruction: ~0.75-0.9M cycles, the largest term by far.
  - dmem stalls (~0.22M) plus load-use/mul-use bubbles (~0.1M). In these
    cycles IF holds the PC and throws away the word the imem bus
    delivered (78% of the time).
  - control: ~51K bimodal branch mispredicts plus ~13.7K JALRs (all
    returns, which always redirect today) at 2 bubbles each: ~0.13M.
A better direction predictor alone cannot pass the 4.6% bar. Even a
perfect one saves only ~3%, and r1s2's trace study found that a 4x
bigger bimodal table removes only ~7K mispredicts. The larger predictor
lever is to use the prediction IF already makes (JAL always taken,
BRANCH via the BHT, plus returns via a new RAS) to let fetch run ahead
of decode. Fetch can then bank the words delivered during backend
stalls and spend them on later imem stalls. The imem and dmem ready
draws are independent, and a flush comes only every ~45 instructions
while an imem stall comes every ~4.5 cycles. So a banked word is almost
always used before a redirect discards it.
(The same direction was drafted in r3s2 but never evaluated. That slot
failed on a sandbox violation, not on the idea.)

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Turn the lock-step IF into a small decoupled, prediction-directed fetch
unit. Add a return-address stack so that returns stop paying the
redirect penalty and stop breaking the run-ahead stream.

1) Fetch queue (FQ) in if_stage.sv: 2 entries in flops, each holding
   {pc[31:0], instr[31:0], pred_taken, pred_tgt[31:2]}, with a 2-bit
   count and a head pointer (or a 2-slot shift register: slot0 = head).
   - fetch_fire = imem_ready && (fq_count != 2) && !redirect. The gate
     uses the REGISTERED count, never this cycle's pop. The PC advances
     to the predicted next PC only on fetch_fire (redirect keeps top
     priority and loads redirect_target). The PC clock enable therefore
     no longer depends on the load-use compare, dmem_ready or ex_busy,
     which takes the hazard unit off the PC/imem-address path.
   - ID source: when fq_count != 0, ID sees the FQ head (valid=1, stored
     pred_taken/pred_tgt). Otherwise ID sees the fetched word directly
     (bypass, valid = imem_ready && !redirect), exactly as today. The
     selected raw word drives the regfile rs1/rs2 read addresses, the
     decoder, imm_gen and the load-use compare.
   - id_accept = the selected source is valid && !stall_id && !flush_id
     (ID/EX really captures it). Pop the head when fq_count != 0 &&
     id_accept. Push the fetched word when fetch_fire && !(fq_count == 0
     && id_accept), meaning it was not consumed through the bypass.
     Clear the count on redirect (wrong-path entries are dropped). ID/EX
     never captures an FQ entry in a redirect_q cycle, because flush_id
     already covers redirect.
   - With the registered-count gate, the steady state after a backend
     stall is one banked word, and each later imem stall consumes it.
     The second entry gives the slack to keep fetching while the head
     is consumed. It also covers the second cycle of multi-cycle dmem
     stalls and divides.
2) Return-address stack: 4 entries x 30 bits (pc[31:2]) in flops with a
   2-bit circular TOS pointer (overflow overwrites the oldest entry). It
   is updated speculatively on fetch_fire only, so each fetched
   instruction touches it exactly once. There is no repair: a corrupted
   entry only costs accuracy, because EX verifies every prediction.
   - Push pc+4 when the fetched word is JAL or JALR with rd in {x1,x5}.
     The pc+4 adder already exists in IF.
   - Predict a return when the fetched word is JALR with rd == x0, rs1
     in {x1,x5} and imm == 0 (GCC's `ret`): pred_taken = 1,
     pred_tgt = RAS[top], next_pc = {RAS[top], 2'b00}, then pop. The
     next_pc mux gains one arm selected by predecode bits: pred_taken ?
     (is_ret ? ras_top : pc+imm) : pc+4.
   - EX (ex_stage.sv), JALR only: mispredict = pred_taken
     ? (misalign_fault || rs1_fwd[31:2] != pred_tgt[31:2])
     : actual_taken. Since only imm==0 JALRs are predicted, the target
     check compares the forwarded rs1 directly with no adder, at the
     same depth as the BEQ comparator, and feeds only the redirect_q
     D input. A misaligned predicted return (rs1[1]=1) therefore
     redirects to pc_next = pc+4 and traps, as today. Unpredicted JALRs
     (function-pointer calls, non-ret forms) still always redirect.
     JAL/BRANCH mispredict logic and pc_next are unchanged.
Expected effect: about 0.2M backend-stall cycles become banked fetches,
and most of them later hide an imem stall (-4..5% cycles). The RAS
removes most of the ~13.7K return redirects (-0.6%). Fmax should be
neutral: the new logic is a flop-selected 2:1 mux in front of
decode/regfile addressing (imem BSRAM DO -> regfile BSRAM AD has large
slack against the 21 ns EX path), and the PC enable gets simpler. The
EX critical path (fwd mux -> ALU -> EX/MEM.alu_result) is untouched;
only redirect_q's D input gains the RAS compare. Net ~+5% fitness.

title: Multiply in EX from ID/EX flops into a registered EX/MEM.mul_result, and flatten the EX result merge so the shifter/adder enter last
motivation:
Gowin timing of the champion (r4s1, place_option 0, 75.6 MHz; median
79.9 MHz, 4,300,957 cycles) shows two path groups, both ending at the
ID/EX operand flops:
  1. 13.19 ns data delay (top 11 of 25 paths): EX/MEM.ctrl.alu_op[2]
     -> 2 LUTs of op decode (mul_a[32] sign bit, fanout 26/72) -> DSP
     A->DOUT (only 3.76 ns) -> 2 LUTs mem_result mux -> 3 LUTs ID
     forward mux -> ID/EX.rs2_val/alu_b. The DSP itself is fast; the
     problem is that it sits between an alu_op decode and the whole
     distance-2 forward network.

     66% of it is routing (3.4 ns first hop), so fewer, wider cells
     also help placement.

acceptance threshold); fixing both should reach about 11.3-11.8 ns.

hypothesis.motivation:
The champion (r4s1, 185.87 = 79.9 MHz x 4,300,957 cycles/10 iter) still
fetches in lock-step with the backend. In every dmem-stall,
load-use/mul-use and divide cycle, IF holds the PC and discards the word
imem delivered, while ~22% of cycles later expose an imem stall as a
bubble. r4s2 measured the fix on a base with the identical hazard
structure and the identical 4,300,957-cycle count: a
prediction-directed 2-entry fetch queue (FQ) plus a 4-entry RAS gave
4,054,468 cycles (-5.7%). It lost because Fmax fell 64.3 -> 62.1 MHz and
sibling r4s1 took the round. LESSONS says to re-apply it on r4s1 and
keep the FQ mux off the new ID-cycle path. A pure direction-predictor
upgrade cannot clear the 4.6% bar: ~51K mispredicts, and a 4x bimodal
removes only ~7K of them.
The champion's Gowin report (generated/timing/gowin_p0) has 20 of its
25 worst setup paths on EX/MEM -> u_mul DSP -> mem_result -> ID fwd
mux -> ID/EX (slack -8.23) and the other 5 on the ID/EX alu_a -> ALU ->
ex_result -> ID fwd mux loop (-7.48). No path from imem DO -> regfile
read -> ID/EX, and no IF/PC path, is among them (all better than
-7.12). So one flop-selected 2:1 LUT in front of decode fits in the
existing slack. The r4s2 Fmax loss is attributed to placement/area, so
this version is built to add as little logic as possible and to keep
every late signal off the wide flop enables.
hypothesis.hypothesis:
Decouple fetch from decode with a 2-entry FQ steered by IF's existing
prediction (JAL taken, BHT branches) plus a new RAS for returns. Words
delivered while the backend is stalled are banked and later hide imem
stalls. The banking ceiling is ~0.78 x ~0.3M backend-stall cycles, and
r4s2 already reached ~0.25M.
1) FQ (if_stage): a circular buffer of 2 entries {pc[31:2],
   instr[31:0], pred_taken, pred_tgt[31:2]} with 1-bit head/tail
   pointers and a 2-bit count, all flops.
   - fetch_fire = imem_ready && count != 2 && !redirect, using the
     REGISTERED count only. The PC loads next_pc on fetch_fire; redirect
     has priority, loads redirect_target and clears count. The PC enable
     therefore no longer sees load-use/dmem/ex_busy (today imem DO ->
     rs compare -> load_use -> stall_if -> PC CE).
   - Data write: entry[tail] <= fetched word on every fetch_fire, whether
     or not ID consumes it. This enable is early. Only tail/count
     (~4 flops) see the late "consumed via bypass" term:
     push = fetch_fire && !(count == 0 && id_accept). Do NOT gate the
     ~190 entry FFs with id_accept/load_use. This is the same trick
     ID/EX uses to keep flush off its data enables.
   - ID source: fq_valid = (count != 0) is a flop. head_word =
     entry[head] is flop-muxed and early. id_word = fq_valid ? head_word :
     imem_data. This single 2:1 is the only logic added on the imem DO
     path, and it feeds the regfile rs addresses, forward_unit, the
     load-use compare, decoder and imm_gen. The ID source is valid
     when fq_valid || (imem_ready && !redirect).
   - pop = fq_valid && id_accept, where id_accept = !stall_id && !flush_id.
     It updates head/count only. Never capture an FQ entry into ID/EX in
     a redirect cycle (flush_id already covers redirect).
2) RAS: 4 x 30-bit flops with a 2-bit TOS, updated speculatively on
   fetch_fire only and never repaired (EX verifies every prediction).
   Push pc+4 on JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5}. Predict a return when the
   word is JALR, rd=x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, imm=0: pred_taken=1, pred_tgt =
   RAS[TOS], pop. next_pc gains one arm: pred_taken ? (is_ret ? ras_top
   : pc+imm) : pc+4. The is_ret decode is shallower than the existing
   pc+imm adder it runs in parallel with.
3) EX (JALR only): mispredict = pred_taken ? (misalign_fault ||
   rs1_val[31:2] != pred_tgt) : actual_taken. rs1_val is an ID/EX flop,
   so this is a 30-bit equality feeding only redirect_q's D input. A
   misaligned predicted return still traps with pc_next = pc+4 and
   redirects. Unpredicted JALRs always redirect, as today.

   flush_id, stall_ex_mem and hold_mem_wb are unchanged.

title: Rebuild the shared ID operand-mux tail: late arms last, pre-decoded load-extract selects, regfile written from MEM (no write-first bypass), per-destination forward selects
motivation:
A fresh `make timing TARGET=bench` probe of the champion (r5s0,
111.4-114.2 MHz, 4,300,957 cycles) finds no single critical path. The top
25 setup paths all fall within 0.11 ns of each other (slack -3.978 to
-3.868 ns, about 8.9 ns of data path after the 5.33 ns clock arrival),
and they come from six different families:
  (a) dmem BSRAM DO (7.59 ns) -> shifted_7 -> load_data_14 -> load_data_31
      -> rs1_fwd_s3 -> rs1_fwd_s1 -> alu_a -> ID/EX.alu_a[28] (8 cells;
      also alu_b/rs1_val/rs2_val)
  (b) ID/EX.rd -> forward compare (5-cell carry chain) -> rs2_fwd_31_s4
      (a shared select net with about 1.2-1.45 ns of fanout routing per
      hop) -> rs2_fwd_3_s2 -> rs2_fwd_3_s0 -> ID/EX.rs2_val (10 cells)
  (c) ID/EX.alu_sub (2.85 ns fanout route) -> b^sub -> adder carry chain
      -> ex_result_29 -> rs1_fwd_29_s1 -> alu_a_29 -> ID/EX
  (d) imem word (the lfsr flop in the bench) -> regfile 32:1 read
      (regs_RAMOUT) -> rs1_fwd_s4 -> s2 -> s1 -> s6 -> ID/EX.rs1_val (4
      tail cells: write-first bypass, x0 check, MEM, EX)
  (e) ID/EX.alu_a -> shifter/logic -> ex_result -> 2 fwd cells -> ID/EX
  (f) ID/EX.alu_b -> SLTU `ult` chain (37 cells) -> ex_result -> fwd ->
      ID/EX
Fixing any one family alone therefore gains close to 0%. What they share
is the tail: every path ends in the per-bit ID operand mux (rs1_fwd /
rs2_fwd / alu_a / alu_b), which costs 2-4 LUT cells plus about 1-1.5 ns
of routing per cell (roughly 3.3-3.7 ns of the 8.9 ns). Synthesis has
put the latest arms (dmem DO, ex_result, the regfile read) at the first
mux level and the early ones (pc/imm, EX/MEM alu/mul flops, the
write-first bypass data) near the D pin.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Rebuild only the operand-mux tail and the arms feeding it, so every late
signal crosses at most 1-2 cells before the ID/EX D pin. Forwarding
distances, interlocks, pipeline depth and IPC do not change (cycles stay
exactly 4,300,957).

1. Late arms last, with the early merge kept as its own net. In id_stage,
   build each of rs1_val, rs2_val, alu_a and alu_b as
     early = pc/const arm | MEM-non-load arm (EX/MEM alu/mul flops) | RF arm
     mid   = sel_ld ? mem_ld : early
     final = sel_ex ? fwd_ex : mid
   Put (* syn_keep *) on `early` and `mid` (per operand) so Gowin cannot
   re-associate the late arms back to the front. fwd_ex (family c/e/f) and
   the forward selects (b) then cross one LUT before the D pin, and mem_ld
   (a) crosses two.

2. Pre-decoded load extract (family a). ex_stage registers one-hot lane
   selects into EX/MEM, computed from agu_sum[1:0] (the first carry-chain
   bits), mem_width and mem_sext: lo_lane[3:0] for result bits [7:0],
   mid_l1/mid_l3 for [15:8], hi_word for [31:16], sg_mid[3:0] (signed
   byte) and sg_hi[3:0] (signed byte/half) sign-fill MSB selects.
   mem_stage builds load_data as a flat AND-OR of the DO bytes with these
   flops (sign = |(sg & lane MSBs)), which removes the >> shifter and the
   width/sext case. mem_stage exports mem_ld (load_data), mem_early

   forward_unit splits the MEM hit into mem_nl and mem_ld.

   (family d). Write regs[] from the MEM stage (w_en = EX/MEM valid &&

   the same edge where MEM/WB captures the instruction. A distance-3
   reader then finds the value already in the array, so reg_file's
   write-first bypass and its rs==0 check go away (regs[0] is never
   written and resets to 0, so it is constant). The RF arm becomes a pure

IF -> IB -> ID -> EX -> MEM -> WB. The fetched word never goes straight
into ID; ID only sees flops, and everything that currently waits in ID for
the raw rs fields is computed one cycle early and registered.

   "ID instruction register"; entry 1 is a skid/overflow slot). IF keeps
   predecode + BHT/JAL prediction on the raw imem word, so predicted-taken
   transfers stay zero-bubble. IF keeps fetching while the queue has room,
   including during load-use, mul-use, dmem-stall and divide holds, so the
   banked words hide later imem stalls. Redirect (redirect_q) flushes both
   entries. Each entry holds pc, instr, pred_taken, valid.

   separately registered, duplicated copies (syn_keep/syn_preserve,
   for example 4 copies each driving 8 regfile words), so the G4 fanout
   route becomes flop -> local route -> 32:1.

   the head, compare its rs1/rs2 (from imem data or entry 1) against the
   rd of the instruction that will be in EX next cycle (the current ID

   in MEM next cycle (the ID/EX occupant if EX/MEM captures it, else
   EX/MEM). Register one-hot hit bits (ex_hit, mem_hit, mem_hit_is_load)

The champion (r5s0: 114.2 MHz median, 4,300,957 cycles, fitness 265.4)

  (c) ID/EX.alu_sub -> b^sub -> adder -> ex_result -> rs1_fwd -> alu_a -> ID/EX

  (e) ID/EX.alu_a -> shifter/logic -> ex_result -> 2 fwd cells -> ID/EX

near the imem-stall ceiling (22% of fetch cycles are lost to imem stalls),

cycles.

title: Prediction-directed IR-headed fetch queue + RAS, with redirect_q steering the imem address directly (no extra redirect cycle, no precomputed selects)
motivation:
The champion (r5s0, 265.42) runs 4,300,957 cycles at 114.2 MHz. It fetches
in lock-step with the backend. During every dmem-stall, load-use/mul-use
and divide cycle, IF holds the PC and throws away the word imem delivered,
and later imem stalls (~22% of cycles) are fully exposed. Three earlier
fetch-queue attempts measured the cycle gain:
  r4s2  comb FQ-head bypass + RAS            4,300,957 -> 4,054,468 (-5.7%)
  r6s2  registered IR-head FQ + RAS          4,300,957 -> 4,098,465 (-4.7%)
Each lost on Fmax, and each for an identifiable reason:
  - r4s2: a combinational FQ-head/imem mux sat in front of the rs fields
    (regfile read, forward and load-use compares). All ID-cycle paths are
    at ~8.9 ns, so one extra LUT there costs ~12%.
  - r6s2: the IR-head fixed that, but it also PRECOMPUTED the forward
    selects one cycle early. Its worst path was ID/EX.alu_op -> is_div ->
    ex_busy -> stall -> FQ pop -> next-entry0 rs mux -> compare ->
    fwd_rs2 flop (13 cells, 101 MHz). This is the same trap that r6s1
    hit (see its LESSONS entry). The IR stage also added one cycle to
    every redirect (~65K mispredicts + JALRs), which accounts for the
    ~44K-cycle gap between r6s2 and r4s2.

branch predictor saves ~51K x 2 cycles (~2.4%). The predictor lever that
can clear it is to use the existing predictions (JAL taken, BHT branches,
plus RAS returns) to let fetch run ahead of decode. The fixes for both
earlier failure modes are now known.

title: Lean prediction-directed fetch-ahead: IR head + 2-slot CE-loaded buffer, redirect_q steers the fetch address, no RAS / no pred_tgt
motivation:
The champion (r5s0, 265.42) runs 4,300,957 cycles at 114.2 MHz. Fetch runs
in lock-step with the backend. On every dmem-stall, load-use, mul-use and
divide cycle, IF holds the PC and discards the word imem delivered, and
later imem stalls (~22% of fetches) are fully exposed. Better direction
prediction alone cannot clear the 4.6% bar. A perfect branch predictor saves
about 51K x 2 cycles (~2.4%), and a RAS saves about 14K JALR returns x 2
(~0.65%). The one predictor-side lever that is large enough is to use the
existing predictions (JAL taken, BHT branches) so that fetch runs ahead into
a buffer.
Three fetch-queue attempts have measured the cycle gain:
  r4s2  comb FQ-head bypass + RAS                 -5.7% cycles, Fmax -3%   (mux on rs fields)
  r6s2  IR-head FQ + RAS + 1-cycle-early selects  -4.7% cycles, Fmax -11%  (stall->pop->compare)
  r7s2  IR-head 3-entry FQ + RAS + imem steering  -5.9% cycles, Fmax -6.7% (congestion)
r7s2 fixed both structural traps: timing showed no pop/stall -> compare path
and no IR redirect bubble. It still lost because the median Fmax fell from
114.2 to 106.6 MHz. The worst path was the pre-existing dmem DO -> load
extract -> ID forward mux -> ID/EX.alu_a path (8 cells, the same as the
champion's), and it was 0.85 ns slower after +433 LUT4 and +326 FF. Most of
that area did not produce the cycle gain:
  - a 4-entry x 30-bit RAS, its push/pop pointer logic, and a 30-bit
    pred_tgt compare in EX;
  - a 30-bit pred_tgt carried in every FQ entry and in ID/EX;
  - a shift-register FQ, where every entry has a D-input mux.
In the timed netlist io_imemData comes from an LFSR flop and io_imemAddr
only feeds the LED XOR (fpga/core_bench_si.sv). The fetch address mux and a
flop-headed ID therefore cost nothing on the critical path. The only
question is how much area the fetch-ahead buffer adds.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Re-apply r7s2's cycle mechanism with the area cut to about a third. The
lesson says to "cut FQ/RAS area first". Use no RAS, no pred_tgt and no
shifting entries.

1. Fetch address steering (if_stage). This is kept from r7s2 and costs
   about 32 LUTs.
   fetch_addr = redirect_q ? redirect_target (EX/MEM.pc_next) : pc_q.
   fetch_addr drives io_imemAddr, the BHT index fetch_addr[7:2], and the
   predecode adders:
     pred_target = fetch_addr + (J ? j_imm : b_imm)
     npc         = pred_taken ? pred_target : fetch_addr + 4
   The redirect target is fetched in the same cycle redirect_q is high, so
   the IR stage adds no redirect cycle. The mispredict penalty stays at the
   champion's 2 cycles.
   fetch_fire = io_imemReady && (redirect_q || count_q != 2). count_q is a
   flop, so no backend stall term enters the fetch enable.
   PC update: pc_q <= fetch_fire ? npc : fetch_addr. A redirect that meets
   an imem stall keeps its target.

2. IR head (the registered ID word). Fields: {pc, instr, valid,
   pred_taken}, 66 flops.
   - ID decodes, reads the regfile, runs the forward/load-use compares and
     generates immediates only from IR flops. No raw io_imemData reaches
     ID, the hazard unit or the forward unit.
   - The champion's IF-side NOP flush mux on the ID instruction is removed.
     An invalid IR simply makes ID/EX capture a bubble (valid = 0,
     ctrl = 0).
   - IR loads with CE = accept | redirect_q | !IR.valid. accept is
     !stall_id && !load_use.
   - IR data D = buf_nonempty ? buf[rd_ptr] : {fetch_addr, imem_data, ...}.
     This is one LUT4/LUT5 level from flops, and the late accept signal is
     only the CE. On redirect_q, IR.valid D = fetch_fire and the buffer is
     cleared. The wrong-path IR word is also turned into a bubble by the
     existing flush_id = redirect.
   - Do NOT precompute anything one cycle early (the r6s1/r6s2 trap).
     Forward selects and load-use stay combinational compares of IR.rs
     against ID/EX.rd and EX/MEM.rd, exactly as today.

3. Two-slot buffer behind IR. It uses write and read pointers; there is no
   shift register and no per-slot data mux.
   - Each slot {pc, instr, pred_taken} is written by CE only:
     slot[wr_ptr] <= {fetch_addr, imem_data, pred_taken} on every
     fetch_fire. wr_ptr always points at a free slot when count_q != 2,
     so the write is harmless when the word goes straight into IR. The CE
     is fetch_fire && wr_ptr == i, which uses only early signals. Only
     count_q and wr_ptr advance based on the late accept.
   - The data inputs are the raw fetch word, so the slots add 0 LUTs of
     data muxing. Only the IR D-mux reads them.
   - count_q, wr_ptr and rd_ptr are small flops. A redirect clears count.
     This gives 2 entries of banking capacity, like r7s2's IR + 2.

   from the champion. No pred_tgt is added to ID/EX.

gives back about 14K x 2 = 28K cycles (+0.65%), so expect about -5.2%
(4.30M -> ~4.08M).

+5-6%.

  (b) Keep reg_file's explicit `rs?_addr == 0` read check (the r7s0/r7s1

      from ID/EX onward is untouched.

title: Shorten all four balanced ID/EX-D-pin path families together: MEM-stage regfile write (no write-first bypass), flop-sourced LUT forward selects, duplicated EX control flops
motivation:
Two timing probes of the champion (r6s0 and r8s0 in log.jsonl) agree that the
paths are balanced: all 25 worst setup paths end at an ID/EX operand D pin
(rs1_val / rs2_val / alu_a / alu_b), lie within 0.1 ns of each other
(~8.9 ns), and fall into four families:
  (1) load:     dmem BSRAM DO -> load extract (3 cells) -> mem_result ->
                rs1_fwd_s3 -> rs1_fwd_s1 -> alu_a -> D
  (2) fwd-sel:  ID/EX.rd -> 5-cell CARRY-CHAIN equality compare against the
                raw imem rs field -> select LUT (fanout 32, 1.45 ns route)
                -> 2 LUTs -> D
  (3) EX loop:  ID/EX.alu_sub (2.85 ns fanout route) -> b^sub -> adder ->
                ex_result -> fwd mux -> D
  (4) regfile:  imem rs bit (4.36 ns route) -> 32:1 flop-mux -> 4 tail cells
                (write-first bypass, x0 check, MEM arm, EX arm) -> D
Fixing one family gains ~0%, which is why the single-family changes (r4s0,
r8s1) scored flat or negative. The full tail rebuilds (r6s0, r7s0, r7s1)
never got timed: they timed out in formal because they dropped the
regfile's explicit x0 read check, and r7s1 moved the mux into EX, which
lost Fmax. Each family still has one cheap local fix that leaves the
champion's ID-side bypass topology, cycle count and x0 check in place.
Doing all of them in one change is the only micro-opt that can move the
balanced front.

Keep the pipeline, hazards and forwarding coverage. The cycle count should
stay bit-identical (4,300,957). Make four local changes, one per family:

A. Family 4: write the regfile from MEM and drop the write-first bypass.
   Write port = (mem_w_en && !dmem_stall, EX/MEM.rd, mem_result), i.e. the
   value MEM/WB captures, written on the same edge. A distance-3 consumer
   then reads the array directly, and no WB forwarding or bypass is needed.
   The regfile read becomes `rs==0 ? 0 : regs[rs]` (KEEP the explicit x0
   check, see r7s0/r7s1: dropping it makes insn_add_ch0 time out). Together
   with the MEM arm, that is one LUT4 per bit
   (regs, x0, sel_mem, fwd_mem), so 32:1 -> LUT4 -> EX/pc arm -> D instead
   of 4 tail cells. MEM/WB data fields (alu_result/read_data) then feed only
   RVFI rd_wdata and get pruned from the timed netlist. wb_stage keeps
   driving the RVFI rd_wdata only. A held load (dmem stall) writes on the
   cycle it completes, and hold_mem_wb still only clears valid.

   keep the compare out of carry chains.

       is always killed by its redirect, or its rd is not written

       bits, early). This removes the EX/MEM.mem_addr -> mem_misalign ->
       mem_w_en logic from the MEM select and from the new regfile write
       enable.

title: Redirect-steered fetch (target fetched in the redirect_q cycle) plus a load-data lane that enters the ID operand mux last
motivation:
The champion (r5s0, 265.42 = 114.16 MHz x 4,300,957 cycles) has two
structural losses, and neither fix adds area to the fetch front end.
That is the property the four fetch-queue attempts lacked (each lost
3-11% Fmax).
  1. Redirect topology. A mispredict found in EX at cycle t is
     registered into redirect_q. At t+1 the PC loads redirect_target,
     but IF still fetches from the stale PC, and that slot is flushed.
     The target is fetched only at t+2. About 65K redirects
     (mispredicts plus all JALRs) each pay this extra slot.
     EX/MEM.pc_next is already a flop at t+1, and in the timed netlist
     io_imemAddr feeds only the LED XOR (io_imemData is the harness
     LFSR flop). So steering the fetch address to the target in the
     redirect_q cycle costs one 2:1 mux on a path that is not critical.
  2. The worst path is dmem BSRAM DO -> byte-lane shift -> sext/width
     mux -> mem_result mux (mem_to_reg / is_mul / alu) -> rs1_other
     mux -> alu_a mux -> ID/EX.alu_a (8 cells, champion critical_path;
     r7s2 had the same path on a different placement). Everything in
     front of the DO pins is flops (EX/MEM.mem_addr[1:0], mem_width,
     mem_sext, mem_to_reg and the forward selects), but the RTL puts
     the late DO through five serial select levels. The load value
     passes through the generic mem_result and rs_other muxes, which
     exist for the early ALU/MUL/regfile sources.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Restructure two stage boundaries without changing the pipeline depth
or the hazard rules.
(A) Redirect-steered fetch (IF). Add
    fetch_pc = redirect_q ? EX/MEM.pc_next : pc. It drives io_imemAddr,
    the BHT index, the predecode target adder (fetch_pc + imm),
    out.pc and pc+4. In the redirect_q cycle the IF slot holds the
    correct target and is valid (flush_if = imem_stall only). ID/EX
    still kills the wrong-path instruction in EX through ex_stage's
    kill, and the load-use compare against that killed instruction
    must be masked by redirect_q so it cannot bubble the correct target.
    PC.D = stall ? fetch_pc : next_pc (from fetch_pc), so a stall in
    the redirect cycle keeps the target. This saves one fetch slot per
    redirect: about 65K cycles (-1.5%). The only addition on the PC
    loop is a 2:1 mux from flops.
(B) Dedicated load-forward lane (MEM -> ID). In EX, register one-hot
    byte-lane / extension selects for the instruction entering EX/MEM.
    They are computed from agu_sum[1:0] (the adder's two LSBs are
    early), mem_width and mem_sext. Examples: sel_b0..3, sel_h0/h2,
    sel_w, sext_b, sext_h. mem_stage then forms load_data per bit as
    a one-hot AND-OR of at most 4 DO bits, and the sign bit as a
    one-hot AND-OR of DO[7/15/23/31]. There is no shift-then-select
    chain. mem_result is split in two:
      mem_fast = is_mul ? mul_result : alu_result   (flops only)
      load_data                                      (DO lane)
    In id_stage the operand mux becomes an AND-OR with early one-hot
    selects: (sel_ex & fwd_ex) | (sel_ld & load_data) |
    (sel_early & {mem_fast / regfile / pc / imm / 4}). forward_unit
    splits the MEM hit into hit_mem_ld (EX/MEM.mem_to_reg) and
    hit_mem_alu. Both fwd_ex and load_data then reach ID/EX through
    the same final level, and every early source is pre-merged
    before it. Cycles, hazards and interlocks are unchanged.
Expected: about -1.5% cycles from (A). For (B), taking about 3 select
levels off the DO path should bring it to or under the EX-loop family,
which r8s1 measured about 0.05 ns behind. That is roughly +2-4% Fmax,
capped by the EX loop, so the total is about +4-5%. Fitness only
improves if (B) does not lengthen the EX loop. The implementer should
run `make timing TARGET=bench` and check that fwd_ex still has a
single level in front of ID/EX.alu_a/alu_b. If fwd_ex gets a level
added in front of it, keep (A) and fall back to taking only the
mem_result merge off the DO path.

title: IF-only predictor upgrade: 4-entry RAS for returns + 256-entry LUTRAM gshare replacing the 64x2 flop BHT
motivation:
The champion (r5s0: 114.2 MHz median, 4,300,957 cycles) pays a 2-cycle
registered-redirect penalty (redirect_q -> PC -> fetch; wrong-path EX slot
killed) on every JALR and every BHT mispredict. r1s2's trace study on the
timed CoreMark region (2.92M instrs) measured: 13,735 JALRs, all of them
returns, which always mispredict today (~27K cycles), and 51,419 mispredicts
with the 64-entry bimodal BHT (~103K cycles). A 256-entry bimodal table
reaches 44,266. Together that is ~130K cycles (~3.0%) of redirect bubbles.
All four fetch-queue attempts (r4s2, r6s2, r7s2, r8s2) lost 3-11% Fmax
because they put logic in front of, or enables on, the ID operand paths.
The champion's timing is a flat wall: the top 25 paths are at 8.83-8.94 ns
and all end at ID/EX operand flops (load align, rd==rs compare,
EX loop, imem-word -> regfile read).
The IF next-PC path (LFSR imem word -> predecode -> pc+imm adder -> PC)
is not in the top 25, so a predictor change that adds logic only to the
PC D-input and keeps its state off the ID paths can win cycles without
touching the wall. The existing 64x2 BHT is 128 flops plus a 64:1 read
mux and 64 update decoders (~200 LUT4). Moving it into Gowin SSRAM
should also free area, which lessons r4s2/r7s2 link to placement pressure.

hypothesis.hypothesis:
Only the direction/target predictor in if_stage changes. The ID/EX operand
paths, forward unit, hazard unit and the registered-redirect mechanism
(redirect_q, kill, penalty) stay as they are.

1. Return-address stack (4 entries x 30 bits, flops, in if_stage).
   - Predecode in IF from the fetched word (same place is_jal / is_br are
     decoded now):
       is_call = JAL/JALR with rd in {x1,x5}
       is_ret  = JALR, rd=x0, rs1 in {x1,x5}, imm==0.
   - Speculative push/pop when the IF slot is really consumed:
     out.valid && !stall_if && !redirect. Push pc+4 on is_call, pop on
     is_ret. Keep a 2-bit TOS pointer. Overflow wraps, and
     a wrong prediction just costs the usual redirect.
   - A return predicts taken with target {ras_top,2'b00}. RAS state is
     all flops, so ras_top only enters next_pc at the last mux level:
       next_pc = pred_ret ? ras_top : pred_taken ? pc+imm : pc+4.
   - Repair: on redirect_q, restore TOS from a checkpoint carried with
     each instruction (2-bit tos in if_id/id_ex/ex_mem, used only on the
     redirect cycle; no comb EX signal reaches IF). Contents are not
     repaired. At CoreMark's call depth with 4 entries that is enough.
   - EX: a JALR carries pred_taken and its predicted target (30 bits in
     ID/EX, or compare against EX/MEM.pc_next next cycle). Mispredict
     for JALR = !pred_taken || pred_target != jump_target. This compare
     feeds only redirect_q's D input, the same as today's mispredict.
     The misalign trap is unchanged: a misaligned JALR target never
     matches a 4-byte-aligned RAS entry, so it redirects/traps as now.
2. Direction predictor: 256 x 2-bit gshare in SSRAM (distributed RAM),
   replacing the 64-entry flop BHT.
   - idx = pc[9:2] ^ ghr[7:0]. ghr is a flop register updated
     non-speculatively from the EX/MEM branch outcome (the same point
     the BHT is trained now), so IF sees a history that is 1-2 branches
     stale. There is no speculative history and no repair.
   - Read: async LUTRAM read from flops (pc, ghr) -> counter[1] ->
     pred_taken. Same depth as the current 64:1 flop mux.
   - The fetch-time idx and the 2-bit counter value ride with the branch
     (if_id -> id_ex -> ex_mem, 10 bits). EX/MEM writes the saturated
     counter +/-1 at the carried idx, so no second read port is needed.
   - The table has no reset. Counter contents are only hints: EX
     checks every prediction, so arbitrary initial values cost a few
     warm-up mispredicts before the start marker and cannot affect
     correctness, formal, or liveness. Do not add a reset or an init
     sweep, because that would force the array back into flops. Check
     that synthesis infers SSRAM (RAM16SDP*), not DFFs. If it doesn't,
     fall back to 128 entries.
Expected cycles: returns ~27K -> ~1K. BHT mispredicts 51K -> ~38-42K
(bimodal-256 alone gives 44K, and gshare usually helps loop-exit
branches). About 50-55K cycles saved (-1.2..-1.3%). Fmax: with no new
ID-path logic and ~-100..-150 LUT4 from moving the BHT to SSRAM, Fmax
should be neutral or slightly positive. The PC D-input gains one 2:1
arm fed by a flop.
Honest ceiling: even perfect direction plus target prediction saves only
~3% cycles at the current 2-cycle penalty. This hypothesis clears the
4.6% bar only if freeing the flop BHT also helps placement of the
8.9 ns ID wall. It is the lowest-risk predictor step, and the
implementer must run `make timing` and report whether any u_if path
enters the top 25.
